name: Concept Universe two-source regex shadow judge corpus v001

items.statement: Regular expressions have been used in system development since 1968.
items.body: Since when have regular expressions been used in system development?
items.answer: They have been part of system development since 1968.

items.statement: The REG-X package for C was created in 1986.
items.body: In what year was the REG-X package created for C?

items.statement: The REG-X package enabled C developers to integrate regular expression matching and manipulation into their programs.
items.body: What did the REG-X package allow C developers to do?
items.answer: It allowed developers to work with regular expressions within their programs.

items.statement: A regular expression is a formal method to specify a text pattern.
items.body: What is a regular expression, in essence?
items.answer: A regular expression (RegExp) is a formal method to specify a text pattern.

items.statement: Regular expressions define patterns that match specific sequences of characters within strings.
items.body: What can regular expressions be used to do with strings?
items.answer: They allow the creation of patterns to select combinations of characters in a string.

items.statement: Special symbols used in regular expressions are called metacharacters.
items.body: What are the special symbols used in regular expressions called?
items.answer: They are called metacharacters.

items.statement: Metacharacters have special meanings that, when combined with normal characters, form a regular expression.
items.body: What makes metacharacters different from normal characters?
items.answer: Metacharacters have special powers (special meanings), and when mixed with normal characters they form a regular expression.

items.statement: Regular expressions enable three kinds of operations that would be difficult with pure programming: validations, replacements, and mask creation.
items.body: What three kinds of operations do regular expressions enable that would be difficult with pure programming?
items.answer: Validations, replacements, and mask creation.

items.statement: Regular expressions can validate common data formats such as dates, times, IP addresses, email addresses, URLs, phone numbers, identification numbers, and credit card numbers.
items.body: List at least five types of data that regular expressions can validate, according to the passage.
items.answer: Dates, times, IP addresses, emails, URLs, phone numbers, CPF, and credit card numbers.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the caret (^) is the metacharacter that anchors a match to the beginning of a line or string.
items.body: What metacharacter is used to mark the beginning of a pattern in a regular expression?
items.answer: The circumflex or caret symbol (^) marks the beginning of a pattern.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the dollar sign ($) anchors a pattern to the end of the string or line.
items.body: What metacharacter is used to mark the end of a pattern in a regular expression?
items.answer: The dollar sign ($) marks the end of a pattern.

items.statement: Unescaped parentheses in a regular expression denote a capturing group.
items.body: In a regular expression, what do parentheses () represent when they are not escaped?
items.answer: Unescaped parentheses represent a group.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the pipe symbol (|) is the alternation operator that matches either the pattern on its left or the pattern on its right.
items.body: What does the pipe symbol (|) do in a regular expression?
items.answer: The pipe acts as an OR operator, allowing for multiple alternative patterns.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the notation [0-9] defines a character class that matches any single digit from 0 to 9.
items.body: What does the notation [0-9] match in a regular expression?
items.answer: It matches any single digit from 0 to 9.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the quantifier {n} immediately following an element means exactly n occurrences of that element must be present.
items.body: What does {2} mean when it appears after an element in a regular expression?
items.answer: It means exactly two occurrences of the preceding element must be present.

items.statement: A developer can add regular expression capabilities to a programming language by using external libraries that provide RegExp support.
items.body: What can a developer do if a programming language does not natively support regular expressions?
items.answer: Use external libraries that provide RegExp support.

items.statement: Regular expressions are natively integrated into text editors like Sublime Text, Brackets, and Vim for searching files and content.
items.body: In what context are regular expressions natively present in tools like Sublime Text, Brackets, or Vim?
items.answer: For searching files or content.

items.statement: In JavaScript, a regular expression literal is delimited by forward slashes (/), not by quotes.
items.body: In JavaScript, how is a regular expression delimited or created — with quotes or with forward slashes?
items.answer: In JavaScript, a regular expression is created using forward slashes (/) instead of quotes.

items.statement: A caret (^) as the first character inside square brackets in a regular expression negates the character class, so the pattern matches any character not listed in the brackets.
items.body: What does the following JavaScript regular expression do: /[^0-9]/ ?
items.answer: It matches any character that is not a digit from 0 to 9, because the caret (^) inside the square brackets negates the group of numbers.

items.statement: In a regular expression, a caret (^) placed immediately after the opening square bracket negates the character class, so the bracket expression matches any character not listed within the brackets.
items.body: What is the meaning of the caret (^) when it appears as the first character inside square brackets in a regular expression?
items.answer: When the caret (^) is the first character inside square brackets, it negates the character set, meaning the expression matches any character that is not in the specified group.

items.statement: In Apache-based web systems like WordPress, the .htaccess file defines URL rewriting rules that control how the server creates and routes human-readable permalinks.
items.body: What purpose does .htaccess serve in a system like WordPress?
items.answer: In WordPress and similar systems, .htaccess defines rules for URL creation and routing.

items.statement: Regular expressions detect varied text patterns in natural language processing, enabling techniques to handle morphological variations such as inflectional forms of words.
items.body: Explain the role of regular expressions in natural language processing (NLP).
items.answer: Regular expressions are a robust and elegant solution for detecting varied patterns in texts, helping NLP techniques handle variations in words with similar meanings — for example, the many forms of verbal and nominal inflection found in Portuguese.

items.statement: Regular expressions help natural language processing systems match words across their morphologically varied forms — such as the diverse inflections of verbs and nouns — that carry similar meanings.
items.body: What challenge faced by natural language processing do regular expressions help solve?
items.answer: The challenge of understanding and interpreting variations in words that carry similar meanings, such as the diverse forms of verbal and nominal inflection in Portuguese.

items.statement: In regular expressions, metacharacters are symbols that carry special syntactic meaning rather than matching themselves literally, enabling both generalized and specific pattern searches.
items.body: Define what metacharacters (metacaracteres) are in regular expressions.
items.answer: Metacharacters are a set of symbols with special properties that allow both generalized and specific searches in regular expressions. Examples include: . [ ] ? * + { } ^ $ \ | ( ).

items.statement: Regular expression metacharacters are classified into four categories: representatives, quantifiers, anchors, and others (including relational metacharacters, grouping, and escape).
items.body: List the four categories into which metacharacters are classified.
items.answer: The four categories are: representantes (representatives), quantificadores (quantifiers), âncoras (anchors), and outros (others, including relational metacharacters, grouping, and escape).

items.statement: In a regular expression, a caret (^) placed immediately after the opening bracket of a character class negates the class, so it matches any single character not listed inside the brackets.
items.body: Given the same four words, state which word(s) match the regular expression '[^csm]ola' and explain why.
items.answer: Only 'Bola' matches '[^csm]ola'. The negated list [^csm] means the first character must NOT be c, s, or m. 'Bola' starts with B, which is not in the excluded set, so it matches. The other words start with c, s, or m and are therefore rejected.

items.statement: A character class in a regular expression can contain multiple ranges, such as a-z and A-Z, written together without a separator to match characters from either range.
items.body: Explain how you would modify '[a-z]ola' so that it also matches words starting with an uppercase letter like 'Bola'.
items.answer: You would include the uppercase range as well, writing the expression as '[a-zA-Z]ola'. This allows the first character to be any lowercase letter a–z or any uppercase letter A–Z.

items.statement: Inside square brackets in a regular expression, a hyphen between two characters denotes an inclusive range spanning all characters between them in the underlying character encoding.
items.body: Explain what the hyphen (traço) means inside square brackets like [a-z] or [0-9].
items.answer: The hyphen indicates a range of values based on the ASCII table. For example, [a-z] is equivalent to listing every lowercase letter from a to z individually, and [0-9] is equivalent to [0123456789].

items.statement: In regular expressions, the dot (.) matches any single character and the asterisk (*) repeats the preceding element zero or more times, so .* matches any sequence of characters (including the empty string).
items.body: Given the words 'Bola', 'cola', 'sola', 'mola', 'ola', 'sol', explain why the pattern .* matches every one of them.
items.answer: The dot matches any single character, and the asterisk says that dot can appear zero or more times. Together, .* matches any sequence of characters, so it returns every element in the list.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the ? quantifier matches the preceding element zero or one time, while the + quantifier matches it one or more times.
items.body: Explain the difference between sol[a-z]? and sol[a-z]+ using the words 'sol' and 'sola'.
items.answer: sol[a-z]? uses the optional quantifier, so the final letter is allowed but not required — it matches both 'sol' (no final letter) and 'sola' (one final letter). sol[a-z]+ uses the plus quantifier, which demands at least one letter after 'sol', so it matches only 'sola'.

items.statement: Anchor metacharacters in regular expressions are zero-width tokens that match a position (such as the start or end of a line or string) rather than any character.
items.body: What is the role of anchor metacharacters in regular expressions?
items.answer: Anchor metacharacters delimit the position of a search within a line or string. They do not match any character themselves; instead, they specify where in the text a match must occur — either at the very start or the very end.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the circumflex (^) negates a character class when placed immediately inside the opening square bracket, and anchors the match to the start of a line or string when used outside square brackets.
items.body: What is the difference between a circumflex (^) used inside square brackets [^ ] and a circumflex used outside square brackets?
items.answer: When the circumflex is inside square brackets, it acts as a list-negation metacharacter, meaning it matches any character not listed. When it appears outside square brackets, it acts as an anchor metacharacter that matches the beginning of a line or string.

items.statement: The `re.match()` function checks for a pattern match only at the beginning of a string.
items.body: Which method from the `re` module checks for a match only at the beginning of a string?
items.answer: The method is `re.match()`.

items.statement: The `re.search()` method scans the entire string for a regular expression pattern and returns the first match object found.
items.body: Which method from the `re` module searches the entire string and returns the first match?
items.answer: The method is `re.search()`.

items.statement: The Python function re.split() splits a string at every occurrence of a regular expression pattern and returns the resulting substrings as a list.
items.body: Which method would you use to split a string at every point where a pattern is found?
items.answer: The method `re.split()` divides the string at the points delimited by the pattern and returns a list.

items.statement: The Python method re.sub() substitutes substrings that match a given regular expression pattern with a specified replacement value.
items.body: Which method replaces parts of a string that match a given pattern with a new value?
items.answer: The method `re.sub()` substitutes part of the string based on the provided pattern with a new value.

items.statement: When splitting text into sentences by a period delimiter, requiring a whitespace character after the dot prevents false splits on abbreviations, decimals, and other period-containing constructs that lack a following space.
items.body: Why is the split pattern \.\s used instead of just \. when splitting a text into sentences, and what problem does it solve?
items.answer: The pattern \.\s looks for a dot followed by a whitespace character. If only a dot were used, sequences like '(EC 3.2.1.21)' would be incorrectly split into four separate sentences. By requiring a space after the dot, the regex avoids these false splits and correctly treats the parenthetical reference as part of a single sentence.

items.statement: Expressões regulares são notações algébricas que representam padrões de caracteres usados para busca e detecção em textos.
items.body: Define expressões regulares (regex).
items.answer: Expressões regulares (also called ER, RE, or regex) are powerful and flexible methods for detecting character patterns. They can be understood as algebraic notations that represent a specific pattern of texts that can be used in a search.

items.statement: A literal search for one form of a word fails to retrieve its inflected variants because inflection changes the word's spelling.
items.body: Using the Portuguese verb "escrever" as an example, explain why a simple literal search is insufficient.
items.answer: A simple search for the word "escrever" would miss its many conjugated forms (escrevo, escreves, escreve, escrevemos, escreveis, escrevem), because each conjugation ends differently.

items.statement: In a regular expression, [a-z] matches any single lowercase letter from 'a' to 'z'.
items.body: Explain what the component [a-z] means in the regular expression `escrev[a-z]{1,4}`.
items.answer: [a-z] is a special character combination meaning any one letter from a to z (lowercase).

items.statement: In a regular expression, {n,m} is a quantifier that specifies the preceding element must occur between n and m times.
items.body: Explain what the component {1,4} means in the regular expression `escrev[a-z]{1,4}`.
items.answer: {1,4} is a quantifier meaning the preceding element ([a-z]) must repeat between one and four times.

items.statement: A regular expression must be general enough to capture all intended variations without being so general that it matches unintended strings, since an imbalance causes either false negatives or false positives.
items.body: Why must regular expressions balance generalization and specificity?
items.answer: A regex must be general enough to capture all intended variations (avoiding false negatives) but specific enough to avoid matching unintended strings (false positives). Without balance, a regex will either miss valid matches or over-match invalid ones.

items.statement: Metacharacters are special symbols (such as ., [, ], ?, *, +, {, }, ^, $, \, |, (, )) with specific meanings that enable generalized and specific searches in regular expressions.
items.body: What are metacaracteres (metacharacters)?
items.answer: Metacharacters are special symbols (such as ., [, ], ?, *, +, {, }, ^, $, \, |, (, )) with specific meanings that enable generalized and specific searches in regular expressions.

items.statement: A representative metacharacter stands in for exactly one other character and must typically be paired with a quantifier metacharacter to match sequences of varying length.
items.body: Explain the role of representative metacharacters (metacaracteres representantes).
items.answer: Representative metacharacters can stand in for other characters and represent exactly one single other character; they often need to be combined with quantifier metacharacters.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the three representative metacharacters are the dot (.) matching any single character, the bracket-enclosed list ([]) matching any one character from a specified set, and the negated list ([^]) matching any one character not in the specified set.
items.body: Name the three types of representative metacharacters described.
items.answer: The three types are: the dot (.), the list ([]), and the negated list ([^]).

items.statement: In a regular expression, the dot (.) matches any single character.
items.body: Given the words 'Bola', 'cola', 'sola', and 'mola', state which words match the regular expression '.ola'.
items.answer: All four words — Bola, cola, sola, and mola — match '.ola'.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the dot (.) matches any single character.
items.body: Explain why the words 'Bola', 'cola', 'sola', and 'mola' all match the regular expression '.ola'.
items.answer: They all match because the dot (.) in '.ola' represents any single character, so any word consisting of exactly one character followed by 'ola' is a match. Each of these four words has one character before 'ola', so they all satisfy the pattern.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the character class [a-z] matches exactly one lowercase letter from a to z.
items.body: Given the same four words, state which words match the regular expression '[a-z]ola'.
items.answer: 'cola', 'sola', and 'mola' match '[a-z]ola' because the pattern requires the first character to be a lowercase letter from a to z.

items.statement: A character class like [a-z] in a regular expression matches only characters within its specified range, case-sensitively, so [a-z] matches lowercase letters only.
items.body: Explain why 'Bola' does not match the regular expression '[a-z]ola'.
items.answer: 'Bola' does not match because 'B' is uppercase and the range [a-z] only includes lowercase letters.

items.statement: The four quantifier metacharacters in regular expressions are * (asterisk), ? (question mark), + (plus), and {x,y} (braces).
items.body: Name the four quantifier metacharacters.
items.answer: The four quantifier metacharacters are: * (asterisk), ? (optional), + (plus), and {x,y} (braces).

items.statement: In regular expressions, the quantifier metacharacters *, ?, +, and {x,y} specify that the preceding element repeats zero or more times, zero or one time, one or more times, or between x and y times, respectively.
items.body: State what each quantifier metacharacter means for repetition.
items.answer: * means zero or more times; ? means zero or one time; + means one or more times; {x,y} means at least x times and at most y times.

items.statement: In a regular expression, a quantifier such as {1,10} applies only to the immediately preceding character or parenthesized group.
items.body: What does the pattern [a-zA-Z]ola{1,10} match?
items.answer: [a-zA-Z]ola{1,10} matches a word that starts with any uppercase or lowercase letter, followed by 'ola', where the 'a' repeats between 1 and 10 times — so it matches 'Bola', 'cola', 'sola', 'mola', and would also match something like 'molaaaaaaaaa'.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the quantifier {n} matches exactly n occurrences of the preceding token, whereas {n,m} matches between n and m occurrences.
items.body: What would happen if you wrote {1} instead of {1,10} in the pattern [a-zA-Z]ola{1,10}?
items.answer: Using {1} instead would require exactly one 'a', so it would match only words like 'Bola', 'cola', 'sola', 'mola' (but not 'molaaaaaaaaa' or anything with extra 'a's).

items.statement: Quantifier metacharacters in regular expressions operate on the element that appears immediately before them.
items.body: What do quantifier metacharacters operate on?
items.answer: The element that appears immediately before them.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the anchor metacharacters are the circumflex (^) and the dollar sign ($).
items.body: Name the two anchor metacharacters.
items.answer: The two anchor metacharacters are the circumflex (^) and the cifrão, or dollar sign ($).

items.statement: The circumflex (^) anchor metacharacter matches the beginning of a line or string.
items.body: Explain what the circumflex (^) anchor metacharacter matches.
items.answer: The circumflex (^) matches the beginning of a line or string.

items.statement: The dollar sign ($) metacharacter in regular expressions matches the end of a line or string.
items.body: Explain what the cifrão, or dollar sign ($), anchor metacharacter matches.
items.answer: The cifrão, or dollar sign ($), matches the end of a line or string.

items.statement: A regular expression beginning with ^ matches from the start of the string, and [a-z]* matches as many consecutive lowercase letters as possible, stopping at the first character outside that class — such as a space.
items.body: Given the string 'rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma', what does the regular expression ^[Rr][a-z]* match?
items.answer: 'rato'

items.statement: In a regular expression, the circumflex ^ is an anchor that forces the match to begin at the first character of the string.
items.body: Given the string 'rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma', explain why the regular expression ^[Rr][a-z]* matches what it does.
items.answer: The circumflex ^ anchors the search to the start of the string. [Rr] requires the first character to be an uppercase or lowercase R. [a-z]* then matches zero or more lowercase letters that follow. So it matches 'rato', the first word.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the anchor `$` matches the position at the end of the string (or line), so a pattern ending with `$` can only match text that reaches the end.
items.body: Given the string 'rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma', what does the regular expression [Rr][a-z]*$ match?
items.answer: It matches 'Roma'.

items.statement: The $ anchor in a regular expression restricts matching to the end of the string, so a pattern like [Rr][a-z]*$ matches only the final word beginning with R or r.
items.body: Given the string 'rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma', explain why the regular expression [Rr][a-z]*$ matches what it does.
items.answer: [Rr] looks for an uppercase or lowercase R, [a-z]* matches any following lowercase letters, and the cifrão ($) anchors the pattern to the end of the string, so only the last word starting with R/r qualifies.

items.statement: The alternative metacharacter (|) in a regular expression matches either the pattern on its left or the pattern on its right, functioning as a logical OR.
items.body: What does the alternative metacharacter (|) do in a regular expression?
items.answer: The alternative metacharacter (|) searches for the character (or pattern) on its right or on its left, acting like a logical OR.

items.statement: In regular expressions, parentheses group multiple characters or alternatives into a single unit that can be quantified, alternated, or captured together.
items.body: What is the purpose of grouping with parentheses () in regular expressions?
items.answer: Parentheses allow searching for groups of characters as a single unit. For example, (rato|Roma) matches the full words 'rato' and 'Roma'.

items.statement: In regular expressions, parentheses group their contents as a single unit for matching, while square brackets define a character class that matches exactly one character from the set listed inside.
items.body: How does grouping with parentheses () differ from using square brackets [] in regular expressions?
items.answer: Parentheses group characters as a single unit (e.g., (rato|Roma) matches the full words), while square brackets define a list of individual characters to match any one of them (e.g., [rato|Roma] matches any single letter like 'r', 'a', 't', 'o', 'R', 'm').

items.statement: In regular expressions, the backslash escape character turns a metacharacter into a literal character, so it matches itself rather than performing its special function.
items.body: What does the escape character (backslash \) do in regular expressions?
items.answer: The escape character (backslash \) converts a metacharacter into a normal literal character, so it can be searched for as itself instead of fulfilling its special function.

items.statement: The shorthand character class \d in regular expressions matches any single digit and is equivalent to the character class [0-9].
items.body: According to the passage (Quadro 5), what does the shorthand character class \d match?
items.answer: \d is equivalent to [0-9] and matches any single digit.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the shorthand character class \w matches any word character: letters (a–z, A–Z), digits (0–9), and the underscore (_).
items.body: According to the passage (Quadro 5), what does the shorthand character class \w match?
items.answer: \w is equivalent to [a-zA-Z0-9_] and matches any alphanumeric character or underscore.

items.statement: The shorthand character class \W matches any character that is not alphanumeric or an underscore.
items.body: According to the passage (Quadro 5), what does the shorthand character class \W match?
items.answer: \W is equivalent to [^\w] and matches any character that is not alphanumeric or an underscore.

items.statement: The shorthand character class \S matches any character that is not a whitespace character.
items.body: According to the passage (Quadro 5), what does the shorthand character class \S match?
items.answer: \S matches any character that is not a whitespace (equivalent to [^\s]).

items.statement: Python's `re` module provides support for working with regular expressions.
items.body: What Python module is used to work with regular expressions?
items.answer: The module is `re`.

items.statement: In Python, the `re` module for regular expressions is loaded with the statement `import re`.
items.body: In Python, how do you load the `re` module for working with regular expressions?
items.answer: With the command `import re`.

items.statement: The Python function `re.findall()` returns a list of all non-overlapping matches of a regular expression pattern in a string.
items.body: What does `re.findall()` return?
items.answer: `re.findall()` returns a list of all non-overlapping matches of a pattern.

items.statement: `re.findall()` returns all non-overlapping matches of a pattern in a string, while `re.search()` returns only the first match.
items.body: How is `re.findall()` different from `re.search()`?
items.answer: Unlike `re.search()`, which returns only the first match, `re.findall()` returns every occurrence.

items.statement: The `re.match` function in Python only finds a match at the beginning of the string.
items.body: What is the result of `re.match("d", "abcde")`?
items.answer: It returns no match (None).

items.statement: The re.match() function only matches a pattern at the beginning of a string.
items.body: Why does `re.match("d", "abcde")` return no match?
items.answer: Because `re.match()` only checks the beginning of the string, and "abcde" does not start with "d".

items.statement: Python's `re.search()` function returns a match object when a match is found.
items.body: What does `re.search()` return when it finds a match?
items.answer: It returns a match object.

items.statement: Indexing a Python `re` match object at 0 returns the entire matched text string.
items.body: How do you print the actual matched text from a `re.search()` result?
items.answer: You can access index 0 of the match object, for example `print(busca[0])`.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the component [a-z0-9]+ matches one or more consecutive lowercase letters or digits.
items.body: Explain the purpose of the part [a-z0-9]+ in the regex pattern [a-z0-9]+@[a-z\.] used for detecting email addresses.
items.answer: [a-z0-9]+ searches for alphanumeric characters (letters and digits) that repeat at least once.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the @ symbol is a literal character that matches only the @ character itself.
items.body: Explain the purpose of the @ symbol in the regex pattern [a-z0-9]+@[a-z\.] used for detecting email addresses.
items.answer: The @ symbol requires that the preceding characters are immediately followed by a literal @, with no spaces or special characters allowed.

items.statement: In a regular expression, the character class [a-z\.] matches exactly one character that is either a lowercase letter or a literal dot.
items.body: Explain the purpose of the part [a-z\.] in the regex pattern [a-z0-9]+@[a-z\.] used for detecting email addresses.
items.answer: [a-z\.] requires the @ to be followed by a set of letters or dots; numbers are not allowed at the end of the email address.

items.statement: In a regex pattern, a character class like [0-9] matches any single character from its set, a quantifier like + means "one or more" of the preceding element, and a literal hyphen - outside a character class matches itself.
items.body: Explain what each part of the regex pattern [0-9]+-[0-9]+ does.
items.answer: The first [0-9]+ searches for numeric characters that repeat at least once. The - requires those digits to be immediately followed by a literal hyphen, with no spaces or special characters allowed. The final [0-9]+ requires the hyphen to be followed by another set of digits that repeat at least once.

items.statement: In Python's `re` module, `match()` finds a pattern only at the start of a string, `search()` finds it anywhere in the string, and `sub()` replaces occurrences with new text.
items.body: What role does each Python method (match, search, sub) play in building a dictionary of abbreviations from text?
items.answer: match() is used to detect the key (the acronym or term) at the start of a match, since it searches only at the beginning of a line. search() is used to find the meaning inside the parentheses anywhere within the matched text. sub() is then used to remove the parentheses from the meaning.

items.statement: Regular expressions were first applied to computers in the 1960s, about 20 years after their mathematical origin in the 1940s.
items.body: How were regular expressions first applied to computers?
items.answer: They were first applied to computers about 20 years after their origin (in the 1960s).

items.statement: QED was the text editor involved in the first application of regular expressions to computers.
items.body: What text editor was involved in the first application of regular expressions to computers?
items.answer: QED, which became one of the first Unix system editors.

items.statement: EGREP is a Linux command-line tool for searching file content by pattern.
items.body: What is EGREP used for?
items.answer: It is a text-mode application for Linux systems used for content searches.

items.statement: To match a literal parenthesis in a regular expression, escape it with a backslash: `\(` matches an opening parenthesis and `\)` matches a closing parenthesis.
items.body: How do you match a literal parenthesis in a regular expression?
items.answer: You must escape the parentheses with a backslash, written as \( and \).

items.statement: In regular expressions, unescaped parentheses are metacharacters that denote a capturing group, so a literal parenthesis must be escaped with a backslash.
items.body: Why can't you just write a parenthesis directly in a regular expression?
items.answer: Because unescaped parentheses are metacharacters that represent a group.

items.statement: In regular expressions, the escaped parentheses \( and \) match literal parentheses, while unescaped parentheses define capturing groups.
items.body: In the DDD regex ^(\([0-9]{2}\)|[0-9]{2})$, the first alternative \([0-9]{2}\) accepts what format of area code?
items.answer: A two-digit number enclosed in literal parentheses, such as (11).

items.statement: In a regular expression, the pattern [0-9]{2} matches exactly two consecutive digits with no other characters around them.
items.body: In the DDD regex ^(\([0-9]{2}\)|[0-9]{2})$, the second alternative [0-9]{2} accepts what format of area code?
items.answer: A two-digit number written without parentheses, such as 11.

items.statement: The .htaccess file is a per-directory configuration file used by the Apache web server to control settings like access, redirects, and URL rewriting.
items.body: What is the .htaccess file?
items.answer: The .htaccess file is a configuration file used by Apache and PHP.

items.statement: The .htaccess file is an Apache web server configuration file that web applications like WordPress use to define URL rewriting and routing rules.
items.body: Which systems commonly use the .htaccess file?
items.answer: It is widely used in systems like WordPress to define rules for URL creation and routing.
